lessons.title: Cutting Metal with Hand Tools: Hacksaws and Shears
lessons.body:
Start with a 24-tooth-per-inch (TPI) hacksaw blade for cutting mild steel. For thin metal under 3mm, use 32 TPI to avoid snagging. For thick stock over 6mm, use 18 TPI. In Africa, you'll often find blades at hardware stores in large cities; if not, salvage from old saws. Secure your metal in a vise or clamp it to a sturdy table. Mark your cut line with a scriber or a permanent marker. For a clean cut, start the saw at a 45-degree angle to create a notch, then bring it flat. Use long, steady strokesâabout 40-50 per minuteâwith light pressure. Let the blade do the work. Too much pressure breaks teeth. Lubricate with a few drops of engine oil or even cooking oil to extend blade life.

For sheet metal up to 1.5mm thick, use tin snips (aviation snips). There are three types: left-cut, right-cut, and straight-cut. For straight lines, use straight-cut snips. For curves, use left or right depending on direction. Hold the sheet firmly and cut close to the vise. Don't cut all the way to the edge in one goâtake small bites. For thicker sheet (up to 2mm), use a bench shear or a chisel and hammer on a hard surface. Always wear gloves; cut edges are razor-sharp.

After cutting, the edges will have burrs. You'll remove those in Lesson 4. For now, focus on accuracy. In many African workshops, a hacksaw and snips are the primary cutting tools. Practice on scrap metalâold car panels, roofing sheets, or bed frames. Measure twice, cut once. A common mistake is cutting too fast and breaking blades. Keep spare blades. If you're cutting pipe, rotate it as you saw to keep the cut straight. Remember: sharp tools are safe tools. Replace dull blades immediately.

lessons.title: Bending and Forming Metal with Hand Tools
lessons.body:
Bending metal by hand requires leverage and control. For thin sheet metal (up to 1.5mm), you can bend it over a sharp edge like a table corner or a piece of angle iron clamped in a vise. For thicker sheet (2-3mm), use a mallet and a formâa pipe or a wooden block. Place the metal on the form and strike it with a rubber or wooden mallet to avoid stretching the metal. For rods and bars up to 10mm diameter, use a vise and a hammer. Clamp the rod in the vise at the bend point, then hammer it over. For tighter bends, use a bending forkâtwo pieces of pipe welded to a handleâor a simple pipe bender.

In Africa, many artisans use a 'bending jig' made from steel pipes welded to a base. You can make one: weld three short pipes (20mm diameter) upright on a steel plate. Space them to fit your rod. Insert the rod between pipes and pull. For curves, use a sandbag or a tree stump as a form. For organic shapes, like leaves, you'll need to stretch and shrink metal. This is done by hammering on a sandbag or a wooden stump. Hammering on a sandbag stretches the metal; hammering on a hard surface shrinks it. Alternate to shape curves.

Always anneal (soften) metal if it cracks. Heat it with a torch until it glows red, then let it cool slowly. For aluminum, heat until a soap mark turns black. For copper and brass, quench in water after heating. Practice on scrap. A common project is a simple hook: bend a 6mm rod 180 degrees over a pipe. Use a vice to hold the pipe. Hit the rod with a hammer near the bend to tighten it. Remember: bend a little, check, bend more. Metal has memoryâit may spring back. Overbend slightly to compensate. Wear safety glasses; metal can snap.

lessons.title: Drilling and Punching Holes in Metal
lessons.body:
For holes up to 10mm in thin metal, use a center punch and a drill. Start by marking the hole with a center punch and a hammer. This creates a dimple to guide the drill bit. Use a drill bit made for metalâhigh-speed steel (HSS) with a 118-degree point. For hard metals, use cobalt bits. Clamp your work securely. If the metal is thin, place a scrap piece of wood underneath to prevent tear-out. Use a drill press if available; otherwise, a hand drill. Run the drill at a slow speed for metalâabout 300-500 RPM for a 6mm bit. Use cutting oil or a few drops of engine oil. Apply steady pressure; don't force it. Let the bit cut. If the bit squeals, slow down and add oil.

For larger holes (over 10mm), use a hole saw or a step drill. A step drill is ideal for sheet metal up to 3mm. It creates multiple sizes. For punching holes, use a hammer and a punch. A hollow punch (also called a wad punch) is used for leather and thin sheet. For metal, use a solid punch and a backing block. Place the metal on a block of lead or hardwood. Strike the punch with a heavy hammer. This works for holes up to 6mm in thin sheet. For larger holes, use a chassis punch or a drill.

In many African workshops, a hand drill is common. If you don't have a drill, you can use a hammer and a nail for very thin metal, but it will be rough. Always deburr holes after drilling. A countersink bit or a larger drill bit twisted by hand can remove the burr. Safety: wear glasses, clamp work, and never hold the work with your hand while drilling. If the bit grabs, it can spin the metal and cut you. Keep bits sharp. Replace when dull.

lessons.title: Filing and Deburring Edges
lessons.body:
After cutting or drilling, edges have burrsâsharp, rough bits of metal. Deburring makes your work safe and professional. Start with a coarse file (bastard cut) to remove large burrs. Then use a smooth file (second cut) for a finer finish. For flat edges, use a flat file. For curved edges, use a half-round or round file. Clamp your work in a vise at about waist height. Hold the file with both hands: one on the handle, the other on the tip. Push the file forward with light pressure; lift it on the return stroke. Don't drag it backâthat dulls the teeth. File at a slight angle to the edge, about 30 degrees, to avoid catching.

For deburring holes, use a countersink bit or a larger drill bit. Turn it by hand or at slow speed in a drill. Just a few turns will remove the burr. For inside curves, use a round file or a half-round file. For outside curves, use a half-round file. In Africa, old files are common; if you can't find new ones, clean the teeth with a file card (a wire brush). Don't use a file without a handleâit can stab your palm. Make a handle from a piece of wood or a cork.

After filing, check for sharp edges with your finger (carefully). A smooth edge should not catch. For a polished finish, use emery cloth or sandpaper wrapped around a file. Start with 80 grit, then 120, then 220. For a mirror finish, use 400 grit and then polish with a buffing wheel. In many workshops, a bench grinder with a wire wheel is used for deburring, but hand filing gives more control. Practice on scrap. A common mistake is filing too much and changing the shape. File a little, check, file more. Keep your files clean and dry to prevent rust.

lessons.title: Using Clamps and Vises for Workholding
lessons.body:
Workholding is critical for safety and accuracy. A bench vise is your most important tool. Mount it securely to a sturdy table. The jaws should be at about elbow height. For holding round stock, use a vise with V-grooved jaws or use a pipe clamp. For flat stock, use the flat jaws. Always tighten the vise firmlyâbut not so tight that you crush thin metal. Use jaw pads (soft jaws) made from wood, aluminum, or copper for delicate work. For long pieces, support the other end with a stand or a clamp.

C-clamps and F-clamps are used to hold work to a table or to clamp pieces together for welding or drilling. For drilling, clamp the work to the drill press table. Never hold work by hand. For welding, use clamps to hold pieces in alignment. In Africa, many artisans use homemade clamps from steel bars and bolts. A simple clamp can be made from a piece of angle iron and a bolt. For holding pipes, use a chain vise or a pipe vise. For holding irregular shapes, use a vise with swivel base or a clamp with a ball joint.

When using a vise, place the work so that the force of the tool is against the fixed jaw, not the movable jaw. This prevents the work from slipping. For sawing, cut close to the vise jaws to reduce vibration. For filing, keep the work low to avoid bending. Always check that the vise is tight before applying pressure. A loose work piece can fly out and cause injury. Use a brush to clean chips from the vise. Lubricate the screw occasionally with oil. In shared workshops, label your clamps. Remember: a good workholding setup makes the job easier and safer.

lessons.title: Project: Metal Leaves and Organic Shapes
lessons.body:
Now you'll combine all the techniques to make a metal leaf. Start with a piece of mild steel sheet, 1mm to 1.5mm thick. Draw a leaf shape (about 10cm long, 5cm wide) on the metal with a marker. Use tin snips to cut out the rough shape. Then use a file to refine the edges and remove burrs. For the stem, use a 6mm rod, about 15cm long. Cut it with a hacksaw. File the ends smooth.

To shape the leaf, place it on a sandbag or a block of wood. Use a ball-peen hammer to stretch the metal in the center, creating a gentle curve. Hammer lightly and evenly. For the veins, use a chisel or a blunt screwdriver to emboss lines. Place the leaf on a soft surface (like a rubber mat) and strike the chisel with a hammer. Move along the leaf to create a central vein and side veins. For a more organic look, bend the edges upward slightly by hammering on the edge over a pipe. This is called 'raising'.

Attach the stem to the leaf. You can weld it, braze it, or use a rivet. For a rivet, drill a 3mm hole in the leaf and the stem, insert a 3mm rivet (or a piece of copper wire), and hammer it flat. If you have a torch, braze with brass rod. For a no-heat method, use a two-part epoxy. In Africa, many artisans use recycled metal from car panels and roofing. Clean the metal with sandpaper before gluing or welding.

To finish, polish with emery cloth and apply a coat of clear lacquer or oil to prevent rust. Make several leaves of different sizes and arrange them on a branch or a wall. This project teaches cutting, bending, drilling, filing, and workholding. Practice on scrap first. A common mistake is hammering too hard and tearing the metal. Work slowly. Your leaf should look natural, not machine-made. Display your work proudly.

quiz.q: What is the recommended tooth count (TPI) for a hacksaw blade when cutting thin metal under 3mm?
quiz.explanation: Thin metal requires a fine blade (32 TPI) to avoid snagging and breaking teeth.

quiz.q: Which type of snips is best for cutting straight lines in sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: Straight-cut snips are designed for straight cuts, while left and right cut snips are for curves.

quiz.q: Why should you lubricate a hacksaw blade while cutting metal?
options: A) To make the cut faster
quiz.explanation: Lubrication reduces friction and heat, extending blade life and improving cut quality.

quiz.q: What is the first step before drilling a hole in metal?
options: B) Mark the hole with a center punch
D) Start the drill at high speed
quiz.explanation: A center punch creates a dimple that guides the drill bit and prevents it from wandering.

quiz.q: When drilling a hole larger than 10mm in sheet metal, which tool is most suitable?
quiz.explanation: A step drill is ideal for sheet metal up to 3mm and can create multiple sizes.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a center punch?
options: B) To create a starting point for a drill
quiz.explanation: A center punch creates a small indentation to guide the drill bit.

quiz.q: Which file cut is used first to remove large burrs?
quiz.explanation: A bastard cut file is coarse and removes material quickly.

quiz.q: How should you hold a file when filing metal?
options: A) One hand on handle, one on tip
quiz.explanation: Holding the file with both hands provides control and even pressure.

quiz.q: What is the correct action when using a file?
options: A) Push and pull with pressure
B) Push with pressure, lift on return
C) Pull with pressure, lift on push
D) Drag back and forth quickly
quiz.explanation: Files cut on the forward stroke; lifting on the return prevents dulling.

quiz.q: Why should you use jaw pads (soft jaws) in a vise?
options: B) To protect delicate work from marks
C) To make the vise stronger
quiz.explanation: Soft jaws prevent the hard vise jaws from denting or scratching the workpiece.

quiz.q: When clamping work for drilling, what is the safest practice?
options: B) Clamp to the drill press table
C) Use a C-clamp on a loose table
D) Ask a friend to hold it
quiz.explanation: Clamping the work to the drill press table prevents it from spinning and causing injury.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of annealing metal before bending?
options: B) To make it softer and less likely to crack
quiz.explanation: Annealing relieves internal stresses and softens the metal, making it easier to bend without cracking.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for bending a 10mm steel rod?
quiz.explanation: A vise holds the rod securely while a hammer provides the force to bend it.

quiz.q: When bending sheet metal over a form, what type of hammer should you use?
quiz.explanation: A soft mallet prevents stretching and marring the metal surface.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a bending fork?
options: C) To bend rods and bars
quiz.explanation: A bending fork provides leverage to bend rods and bars accurately.

quiz.q: How can you tell when aluminum is annealed?
options: B) A soap mark turns black
quiz.explanation: When heating aluminum, a soap mark turns black at the annealing temperature.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of not deburring edges?
quiz.explanation: Burrs are sharp and can cause serious cuts; deburring makes the edge safe.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to remove a burr from a drilled hole?
quiz.explanation: A countersink bit chamfers the hole edge and removes the burr.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to store files?
options: B) In a drawer with other tools
C) Clean and dry, separate from other tools
quiz.explanation: Files should be kept clean and dry, and not banged against other tools to preserve the teeth.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a file card?
quiz.explanation: A file card is a wire brush used to clean metal chips from file teeth.

quiz.q: When using a vise, which jaw should the force of the tool be against?
quiz.explanation: The fixed jaw is stronger and prevents the work from slipping.

quiz.q: What is a common material for making homemade clamps in African workshops?
quiz.explanation: Steel bars and bolts are readily available and strong enough for clamps.

quiz.q: Why should you support the far end of a long workpiece?
options: A) To prevent bending and vibration
B) To make it look neat
quiz.explanation: Support prevents the work from sagging, bending, or vibrating during cutting or drilling.

quiz.q: What is the first step in making a metal leaf?
options: B) Draw the shape on metal
quiz.explanation: You need to mark the shape before cutting and forming.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to emboss veins on a metal leaf?
quiz.explanation: A chisel or blunt screwdriver struck with a hammer creates indented lines.

quiz.q: What is 'raising' in metal shaping?
options: A) Hammering the edge over a pipe to bend it upward
quiz.explanation: Raising is a technique to curve the edges of a metal sheet by hammering over a form.

quiz.q: How can you attach a stem to a leaf without welding?
options: A) Use a rivet or epoxy
quiz.explanation: Rivets or two-part epoxy are effective cold-connection methods.

quiz.q: What is a common source of recycled metal for projects in Africa?
options: A) New sheets from hardware stores
B) Car panels and roofing sheets
quiz.explanation: Car panels and roofing sheets are commonly recycled for metal sculpture.

quiz.q: What should you apply to a finished metal leaf to prevent rust?
quiz.explanation: A protective coating like lacquer or oil prevents oxidation.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when hammering metal for organic shapes?
options: A) Hammering too hard and tearing the metal
quiz.explanation: Excessive force can stretch or tear thin metal; light, controlled blows are better.
